name: Award subcontracts and purchase orders (buyout)
summary: After a project is won, the general contractor turns each trade bid carried in its price into a signed subcontract. For each of about 25 packages per project the team re-levels the bids against the final contract, checks the bidder is prequalified, holds a scope review meeting, gets a final price, approves the award, checks insurance and bonds, drafts and signs the subcontract and enters it in the ERP as a commitment. Buyout gains or losses against the estimate set the project's early margin. It is slow because subcontractors take days to reprice, sign and send certificates, and error-prone because scope that falls between trades is easy to miss.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian national general contractor of about 2,800 employees that subcontracts most trades and awards about 25 subcontracts per project.
baseline.notes: Bids were levelled in Excel, subcontracts drafted from a company standard form in Word or the ERP and signed by PDF or e-signature. Purchase orders for major materials follow a similar but shorter path in material procurement and are not modelled here.

trigger: A trade package is released for buyout from the project's buyout plan in the startup package.
end_state: The subcontract is signed by both parties, entered in the ERP as a commitment and distributed to the site and accounts payable; or the package is re-tendered or self-performed.

volume.seasonality: Follows project starts: heaviest from March to June, light in December.

evidence.note: Organisation file: about 10 project starts a month x about 25 trade packages per project.

surge.cause: spring start of the construction season with several projects buying out at once

evidence.note: Follows the spring bunching of project starts; author's estimate.

systems.name: Take-off and estimating software with Excel bid sheets
Subcontractor prequalification database (questionnaires, insurance and WSIB certificates)
Government portals (WSIB clearance, Ministry of Labour notice of project, CRA, land registry)
Construction ERP (job cost, general ledger, payables, receivables, payroll)
Reporting and dashboards (Excel cost reports, Power BI)
Project management platform (drawings, RFIs, submittals, daily logs, change events)

steps.name: Open the trade package in the buyout log
steps.description: The subcontract administrator takes the next trade package from the project's buyout plan, enters it in the buyout log with its budget, scope sheet, required award date and the bidders from tender, and opens a package folder. Packages are released in waves following the construction sequence.

error.defect_description: Wrong budget line attached to the package.

evidence.note: Waves by trade sequence over the first four weeks after award; the wait spreads packages over that period.

steps.name: Pull the tender bids and leveling sheet
steps.description: The subcontract administrator retrieves the trade bids received on bid day, the estimator's leveling sheet and any bid depository or portal records from the estimating files, and checks how many compliant bids the package has.

error.defect_description: A late addendum price or alternate is not picked up.

steps.name: Re-level bids against the contract documents
steps.description: The assistant project manager compares each bidder's inclusions, exclusions and qualifications with the final contract drawings, specifications and addenda line by line, prices the holes so every bid covers the same scope, and flags scope that falls between two trades.

error.defect_description: A scope gap between trades is missed and later becomes a change order.

evidence.note: Bid normalising and scope gap checks.

steps.name: Check prequalification of the low bidders
steps.description: The prequalification analyst looks up the two lowest bidders in the prequalification database: safety record (experience modification rate, COR status), WSIB clearance, insurance, bonding capacity and the dollar limit approved for that trade. She replies with pass, conditional or fail.

error.defect_description: An expired insurance certificate in the database is not noticed.

control.basis: Company subcontractor prequalification policy (safety, financial and bonding limits)

evidence.note: EMR above 1.00 and bond rate above 2.5% flag risk in the source.

steps.name: Subcontractor submits prequalification documents
steps.description: The bidder that is not on file, or whose file has expired, completes the questionnaire and sends financial references, safety statistics, COR certificate, insurance and WSIB documents, which then return to the analyst for checking.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: Small subcontractors often take one to two weeks to assemble prequalification documents.

steps.name: Shortlist bidders and set negotiation strategy
steps.description: The project manager reviews the re-levelled comparison and prequalification results, shortlists one or two bidders, and decides what to clarify: schedule, crew size, exclusions and alternates. Where a bid depository applies he must use the carried bidder unless there is a reasonable objection.

error.defect_description: Shortlists a bidder whose number excludes major scope.

control.basis: Bid depository rules and company ethics policy against bid shopping

evidence.note: Shortlist of 1-2 per package; no bid shopping.

steps.name: Book the scope review meeting
steps.description: The subcontract administrator calls the shortlisted bidder's estimator and project manager, agrees a time for a scope review meeting at the office or by Teams, and sends the scope sheet, draft schedule and standard subcontract terms in advance.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

steps.name: Hold the scope review meeting
steps.description: The project manager walks the bidder through the scope sheet line by line, confirms exclusions, schedule and manpower, safety requirements, insurance, holdback and payment terms, and asks the bidder to price any gaps. He states that the standard subcontract terms are not negotiable.

error.defect_description: A clarification is agreed verbally but not written down.

steps.name: Write and issue the meeting minutes
steps.description: The subcontract administrator writes the scope clarifications, inclusions, exclusions and action items into minutes, sends them to the bidder within a day and asks for a revised price on that basis.

error.defect_description: Minutes word a clarification differently from what was agreed.

evidence.note: Minutes within 24 hours.

steps.name: Subcontractor returns the final price
steps.description: The bidder reprices the clarified scope, adds or removes items and returns a best and final price, often with new qualifications attached.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: Best and final offer after scope clarification.

steps.name: Evaluate the final price against budget and decide
steps.description: The project manager compares the final price with the package budget and the next bidder, records the buyout gain or loss, and decides to award, negotiate again, or re-tender the package or self-perform it. Awards above his limit or over budget go to the operations manager.

error.defect_description: Buyout variance calculated against the wrong budget line.

next.condition: over his signing limit or over budget
no acceptable bid: re-tender or self-perform

evidence.note: Branch shares are the author's estimate; larger packages (mechanical, electrical, structure) usually exceed a project manager's limit.

steps.name: Approve the award
steps.description: The operations manager reviews the recommendation, the buyout variance and the bidder's risk profile, and approves the award or sends it back for more negotiation. Higher-risk subcontractors get a closer look before award.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

control.basis: Company delegation of authority for subcontract awards by value and budget variance

evidence.note: Directors review risky subcontractors before award.

steps.name: Check insurance, WSIB clearance and bonds
steps.description: The subcontract administrator checks that the subcontractor's insurance certificate names the company and owner with the required limits, downloads a current WSIB clearance certificate, and confirms whether performance and labour and material payment bonds are required for this package.

error.defect_description: Additional insured wording missing but accepted.

control.basis: Company subcontract policy and prime contract insurance requirements (CCDC 2-2020 GC 11.1 flowed down)

evidence.note: Insurance certificates before signing.

steps.name: Chase missing certificates or bonds
steps.description: The subcontract administrator emails and phones the subcontractor's office or broker for the missing insurance certificate, WSIB clearance or bond, and notes the request in the buyout log.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: Common Canadian general contractor buyout practice; durations are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Subcontractor supplies certificates or bonds
steps.description: The subcontractor's broker issues the certificate, or its surety issues the bonds, and sends them back; bonds take longest because the surety reviews the subcontract value.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: Broker certificates take a day or two; surety bonds one to two weeks.

steps.name: Draft the subcontract
steps.description: The subcontract administrator fills the company's standard subcontract form in the ERP or Word: parties, price, scope schedule from the minutes, unit rates, schedule dates, holdback, insurance and safety requirements, and the prime contract terms that flow down.

error.defect_description: Scope schedule attached is the bidder's original proposal, not the agreed minutes.

control.basis: CCDC 2-2020 GC 3.6.1 (subcontracts must incorporate the prime contract terms)

steps.name: Review the subcontract for non-standard terms
steps.description: The supply chain manager reads the draft against the standard form and the minutes, checks scope wording, price and bonding, and sends any changed clauses or subcontractor-proposed terms to legal.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

control.basis: Company policy: subcontracts reviewed by supply chain before signature

evidence.note: Common Canadian general contractor buyout practice; durations are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Legal review of changed terms
steps.description: Contracts counsel reviews the clauses the subcontractor changed (limitation of liability, warranty, payment, design responsibility) and marks acceptable wording or a fallback position.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: About 12% of subcontracts carry non-standard terms that go to legal; author's estimate.

steps.name: Sign the subcontract for the company
steps.description: The project manager, within his signing authority, signs the subcontract for the company after a final check that price and scope match the approved award.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: Common Canadian general contractor buyout practice; durations are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Send the subcontract for signature
steps.description: The subcontract administrator sends the signed subcontract to the subcontractor by email or e-signature with a cover note listing what must come back: signed copy, schedule of values and safety documents.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: Common Canadian general contractor buyout practice; durations are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Subcontractor reviews and signs
steps.description: The subcontractor's office reviews the subcontract, often with its own lawyer or bonding company, and either signs it and returns the schedule of values or sends back markups on clauses it will not accept.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: Common Canadian general contractor buyout practice; durations are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Negotiate the subcontractor's markups
steps.description: The subcontract administrator collects the markups, gets the project manager's and if needed counsel's position on each, and agrees final wording with the subcontractor by phone and email before re-issuing.

error.defect_description: Agreed wording not carried into the re-issued copy.

evidence.note: Common Canadian general contractor buyout practice; durations are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Enter the commitment in the ERP
steps.description: The subcontract administrator enters the subcontract in the ERP as a commitment against the project's cost codes, with schedule of values lines and holdback percentage, so invoices can be matched and the cost report shows committed cost.

error.defect_description: Commitment coded to the wrong cost code.

evidence.note: Common Canadian general contractor buyout practice; durations are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Request vendor setup for a new subcontractor
steps.description: For a subcontractor not yet in the ERP, the subcontract administrator sends a vendor setup request with legal name, address, HST number, banking form and WSIB number to the vendor master team.

error.defect_description: Banking form missing.

evidence.note: Common Canadian general contractor buyout practice; durations are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Update committed cost and buyout log
steps.description: The ERP posts the commitment to the job cost report and the buyout log spreadsheet picks up the committed amount and variance for the package.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

steps.name: Distribute the executed subcontract
steps.description: The assistant project manager files the executed subcontract in the project platform, sends copies to the superintendent and accounts payable, adds the trade to the directory and opens its submittal register.

error.defect_description: Accounts payable not sent a copy, so the first invoice is held.

evidence.note: Common Canadian general contractor buyout practice; durations are the author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Bidder not prequalified
exceptions.description: The low bidder is not in the database or its file has expired; it has to submit documents before the award can proceed.

exceptions.name: Second round of negotiation
exceptions.description: The final price still excludes scope or exceeds budget, so another scope meeting is held.

exceptions.name: Missing insurance, clearance or bonds
exceptions.description: Certificates or bonds are missing or expired and the award waits for the broker or surety.

exceptions.name: Subcontractor marks up the terms
exceptions.description: The subcontractor returns the subcontract with changed clauses that have to be negotiated and re-issued.

exceptions.name: Package re-tendered or self-performed
exceptions.description: No acceptable price can be reached and the package goes back to tender or to the self-perform group.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from package release to executed subcontract

evidence.note: Sources: 90% of work bought out within 2-4 weeks; 2-4 weeks typical and 6-8 weeks on large projects; 2-6 weeks, 4-6 with 20+ packages. These describe the whole project's buyout; per-package p50 and p90 are the author's reading of them.

benchmarks.population: One US general contractor's internal standard

pain_points.description: Scope that falls between two trades is missed when bids are levelled in a hurry and returns months later as a change order.
Awards wait on subcontractors' brokers and sureties for certificates and bonds.

evidence.note: Get certificates before signing, not after.

pain_points.description: Subcontractors take days to reprice and sign, and some return markups that restart the signing loop.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common practice.

pain_points.description: The buyout log is a spreadsheet kept apart from the ERP, so committed cost and buyout variance are re-keyed.

evidence.note: Common 2019-2022 practice.

sources.title: Buyout (Brinkmann Constructors process database)
sources.publisher: Procore Technologies support site, Brinkmann Constructors process pages
sources.supports: Bid analysis and normalising, buyout meetings with each bidder's estimator and operations lead, minutes issued within 24 hours, review of EMR (above 1.00 flags safety risk) and bond rate (above 2.5% flags financial risk), confirmation of insurance and payment terms, director review of risky subcontractors before award, call the number 2 bidder first, then issue subcontracts and purchase orders; typically 90% of the work is bought out within 2-4 weeks depending on project size.

sources.title: Construction Buyout Process Guide
sources.supports: Buyout in weekly waves after award (long-lead and early trades in week 1, structure and MEP week 2, interiors week 3, specialties week 4); bulk of buyout takes two to four weeks on a typical commercial project and six to eight weeks on larger ones; verify insurance certificates before signing the subcontract; scope gaps between bids become change orders.

sources.title: Construction Buyout: How GCs Finalize Subcontract Awards After Bid Leveling
sources.supports: Buyout steps after leveling: buyout log, letters of intent for long-lead items (16-36+ week lead times), shortlist of 1-2 subs per package, scope clarification meetings, best and final offers, executed subcontracts; buyout typically takes 2-6 weeks after award, 4-6 weeks with 20+ trade packages; unresolved scope gaps turn into change orders.

sources.title: CCDC 2 - 2020 Stipulated Price Contract (standard form text in a District of Hudson's Hope tender package)
sources.publisher: Canadian Construction Documents Committee; document posted by the District of Hudson's Hope
sources.supports: GC 3.4.1: construction schedule submitted to owner and consultant before the first application for payment, showing major activities and critical events, monitored and updated monthly or as the Contract Documents state, consultant advised of revisions from extensions of Contract Time; GC 3.6.1: contractor makes written agreements with subcontractors and suppliers that incorporate the prime contract terms; GC 3.6.2-3.6.3: owner may object to a proposed subcontractor before signing; GC 5.2.4: schedule of values at least 15 calendar days before the first application for payment; GC 9.4.1: contractor establishes, maintains and supervises health and safety precautions and programs; GC 10.4.1: evidence of workers' compensation compliance before commencing the Work and with each application for payment; GC 11.1: contractor insurance per CCDC 41.

assumptions: The case is one trade package from release for buyout to executed subcontract. Material purchase orders are handled by scm-material-procurement and not counted here.

The wait at s01 spreads packages over the first two to four weeks after the startup package, following the trade sequence; it is part of the cycle time because the clock starts at release of the startup package.

Bid re-levelling at buyout is done by the assistant project manager; the organisation file's process roles list assistant-pm already, but omit prequal-analyst, operations-manager (award approval), and contracts-counsel (non-standard terms), which are used here.

fte_on_process for each role = mean hands-on hours per case from the steps x 250 awards a month / 130 productive hours, plus 20% for calls and email not written as steps. This puts about 16 of the 22 subcontract administrators on buyout; the rest handle purchase orders and subcontract changes.

The simulated median (about 26 days) is above the 21-day per-package benchmark because the sources describe 90% of value bought out in 2-4 weeks, with the large early packages moving fastest, while the simulation weights every package equally including small late ones.
Bid depository rules apply to some public projects in Ontario; the shortlist step carries that control. Branch shares are tier C estimates.
